title: Why AI gets things wrong
blurb: How a model can sound confident and still be mistaken.

slides.title: Confident isn’t the same as correct
body: Sometimes a model states something false as if it were fact. This is often called a “hallucination”.
A model writes what is likely to come next, so a wrong answer can be just as fluent and confident as a right one. The tone tells you nothing about accuracy.

visual.caption: Illustrative example. Invented references are a well-known failure mode.
visual.question: Can you give me a source for that?

cards.label: What you might see
cards.text: A tidy reference with authors, a title, a journal and a year.

cards.label: What may be true
cards.text: The paper doesn’t exist — it was pieced together from the patterns of real references.

slides.title: Why it happens
body: Nothing in the prediction step checks facts. When the model’s training gives it a clear answer, it usually gets things right.
When it doesn’t, it still produces an answer-shaped reply, because that’s what usually comes next.

visual.caption: Common causes — often several at once.

items.heading: Gaps in training
items.text: Rare topics, niche details and specific numbers were seen too little to learn reliably.

items.heading: Out-of-date knowledge
items.text: Training stops at a cut-off date, so recent events may be missing or wrong.

items.heading: Pressure to answer
items.text: Saying “I’m not sure” is less common in text than giving an answer, so models tend to answer.

slides.title: Giving it the source helps — but doesn’t guarantee
body: Putting the facts in the context window — a pasted document, say — gives the model something to draw on instead of guessing.
It can still misread the source or mix in things from elsewhere, so the answer still needs checking. It’s just much easier to check.

visual.caption: When the answer can come from the pasted source, there’s less room for guessing.

slides.title: How to check its work
body: AI can save a lot of time, but you’re still responsible for what you do with its answers.
The more an answer matters, the more it’s worth checking.

visual.caption: Good habits for any AI tool.

items.heading: Open the sources
items.text: If it cites something, check the source exists and says what it claims.

items.heading: Verify the specifics
items.text: Names, numbers, dates and quotes are where errors hide.

items.heading: Treat it as a draft
items.text: Use the answer as a starting point, not a final decision.

quiz.question: What does “hallucination” mean for an AI model?
options: The model crashes and stops responding
The model states something false or made up as if it were fact
quiz.explanation: A hallucination is confident-sounding output that isn’t true, such as a made-up fact or reference.

quiz.question: Why might a model invent a reference that doesn’t exist?
options: It writes text shaped like a reference without checking that one exists
It is trying to trick you
The reference was deleted from the internet
quiz.explanation: The model has learned what references look like, so it can produce a convincing one — but nothing checks that it’s real.

quiz.question: You’re using an AI answer for something important. What’s the best approach?
options: Trust it if it sounds confident
Ask the same question again until the answers match
Check the key facts against reliable sources
Lower the temperature so it can’t be wrong
quiz.explanation: Confidence and consistency aren’t evidence. Checking key facts against reliable sources is what catches errors.
